Pregnancy

Is my baby head down? Position clues, checks and birth options

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Kicks and changes in your bump can make you curious about how your baby is lying. Your maternity team can confirm the position and explain whether it matters for your stage of pregnancy.

Head down, breech and sideways: what the words mean

A baby’s presentation describes which part is nearest the birth canal. In a head-down, or cephalic, presentation, the head is lowest. In a breech presentation, the bottom or feet are lowest. A transverse lie means the baby is lying across the uterus rather than lengthways.

Position is a related but different description: a head-down baby may face toward your back or toward your front. Engagement means the head has moved down into the pelvis. A baby can be head down without being engaged, and neither finding tells you exactly when labour will begin.

When babies usually turn

Babies change their lie often earlier in pregnancy. A breech baby in the late second or early third trimester may turn without intervention. By the end of pregnancy only about 3–4 in 100 babies remain breech. An early scan is therefore a description of that moment, not a final birth plan.

If the baby is still breech at around 36 weeks, your maternity team will discuss confirmation and options. There is no exact day by which every baby must turn. Although space becomes tighter as pregnancy progresses, this does not make reduced movement normal: you should still feel your baby moving up to and during labour.

What anterior and posterior positions mean

In an occipito-anterior position, the back of a head-down baby’s head points toward the front of your pelvis. The baby generally faces your back, often with the chin tucked. In an occipito-posterior position, the back of the head points toward your back instead.

A posterior baby can be associated with back pain or a longer labour, but many rotate during labour, and some are born facing forward. Depending on progress and wellbeing, assistance with rotation, forceps, a vacuum device or a caesarean may be considered. A posterior position on its own does not mean a vaginal birth is impossible.

How your maternity team checks

A midwife or doctor can gently feel the abdomen to estimate where the head, back and bottom are. A head may feel like a firm round part low down, with the bottom higher up, but interpreting the examination takes training. The assessment can be less clear in some pregnancies.

If there is uncertainty, or a breech or transverse lie is suspected near the end of pregnancy, ultrasound can confirm it. In labour, an examination may provide further information when clinically appropriate and with your consent. Ask what was found and whether it changes your next appointment or birth plan.

What kicks, hiccups and the shape of your bump can tell you

Strong kicks high in the abdomen, smaller movements lower down and pressure in the pelvis may make you wonder whether the baby is head down. Rhythmic hiccups may be felt in different places. These sensations can be interesting to notice, but they are not a dependable way to identify the head or distinguish hands from feet.

The baby’s angle, your posture, the placenta and how movement is transmitted through the uterus can all affect what you feel. A different bump shape or a new location for kicks is not enough to decide that the baby has turned. Describe the change at your appointment rather than treating a home guess as confirmation.

Belly mapping is not a diagnostic test

“Belly mapping” usually means sketching where you think you feel the baby’s back, limbs, head and bottom. Some people enjoy using a drawing or doll to picture the baby. It cannot establish the presentation reliably or replace an examination before a decision about birth.

You do not need to press deeply on your abdomen, repeatedly search for a hard round part or lie flat for a mapping exercise. Never try to turn the baby yourself or have an untrained person push on your abdomen. If mapping makes you worried or uncomfortable, stop and ask your maternity team to explain the position at a visit.

Do not use a home Doppler to decide the position or wellbeing

Where you hear a sound with a home Doppler is not a reliable way to locate the baby’s head. It can also be difficult to distinguish the baby’s heartbeat from other sounds. Hearing a heartbeat does not show that the baby is well.

If movements become fewer, stop or change from your baby’s usual pattern, contact your maternity service immediately. Do not wait until the next day, keep trying the Doppler or explain the change away as the baby turning. A professional assessment addresses a different question from simply hearing a sound.

If the baby is still breech late in pregnancy

The team will consider the exact presentation, pregnancy stage, placenta, fluid around the baby, your health and the baby’s wellbeing. Earlier in pregnancy, waiting and reassessing is often appropriate. Later, the discussion becomes a plan for turning the baby when suitable and deciding how and where to give birth.

Options commonly include external cephalic version, known as ECV, a planned caesarean, or a planned vaginal breech birth in selected circumstances. You should have time to discuss the benefits and disadvantages, and what happens if labour begins before the planned date. Having a breech baby is not something you caused by sitting or sleeping the wrong way.

What happens during ECV

ECV is an attempt by a trained clinician to turn the baby through controlled pressure on your abdomen, usually around 36–37 weeks. It is carried out in a hospital where an emergency caesarean can be performed if necessary. Ultrasound and fetal-heart monitoring are used before and after the attempt.

You may receive medicine to relax the uterus; it can briefly cause flushing or palpitations. The manoeuvre can be uncomfortable, and you can ask for it to stop. It succeeds in roughly half of attempts, with individual chances varying. Another attempt may sometimes be offered, and a small proportion of babies turn back afterward.

Who can have ECV, and what follow-up is needed?

ECV is not appropriate in every pregnancy. Reasons against it can include a placenta covering the cervix, recent bleeding, concerning fetal-heart monitoring, ruptured membranes or a multiple pregnancy. The team reviews your own circumstances rather than applying a home checklist. If you are RhD-negative, they will consider anti-D protection according to your care plan.

Serious complications are uncommon, but an emergency caesarean is needed after about 1 in 200 attempts, which is why the hospital setting matters. Follow the discharge advice and contact the maternity team promptly about bleeding, abdominal pain, contractions, broken waters or reduced movements afterward. A successful turn still needs ordinary antenatal follow-up.

Choosing between caesarean and vaginal breech birth

For a baby that remains breech at term, a planned caesarean generally lowers the baby’s immediate birth risks compared with a planned vaginal breech birth. It is also abdominal surgery, with risks such as infection, bleeding and blood clots, and possible implications for future pregnancies, including placental problems or the uterine scar opening.

A vaginal breech birth may be considered for selected pregnancies with an experienced team and immediate access to emergency surgery. The type of breech, estimated size, head position and other pregnancy factors matter. Even with a vaginal plan, a caesarean may become necessary. Ask about the local team’s experience and the options available to you; one percentage from another setting cannot describe your own chances.

If the baby is sideways, or symptoms start before your plan

A baby that remains transverse near birth usually needs a different delivery plan, commonly a caesarean if turning is not possible or unsuccessful. Your team may discuss admission before labour in some circumstances. When the presenting part does not fill the pelvis, there is more room for the umbilical cord to slip down after the waters break.

Contact your maternity unit urgently if your waters break, you bleed, movements reduce or you think labour has started: especially with a known breech or transverse baby. If you see or feel a cord in the vagina, call emergency services immediately and do not try to push it back. Follow the emergency team’s instructions. Keep your maternity number and agreed plan somewhere easy to find.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Home sensations and Dopplers cannot reliably establish fetal position or reassure about reduced movements.

A breech presentation late in pregnancy calls for individual discussion of ECV and birth options.

How BeMama can help

Ask your midwife to explain the baby’s presentation and record the next step in your birth plan.

When to seek help

Contact maternity care immediately for reduced or changed movements, broken waters or bleeding. A visible or felt prolapsed cord is an emergency.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Head down, facing direction and engagement describe different things.
  • Many babies turn naturally before the end of pregnancy.
  • Kicks and hiccups are clues, not confirmation.
  • ECV is a monitored hospital procedure, never a home manoeuvre.
  • Keep a clear plan for labour or broken waters before a planned delivery.

Frequently asked questions

Do kicks under my ribs prove my baby is head down?

No. Where you feel movement cannot reliably identify each body part. Your midwife or doctor can examine you and use ultrasound when confirmation is needed.

Do hiccups below my belly button prove the head is low?

No. The place where you feel hiccups can vary and is not a diagnostic sign. Ask about presentation at your antenatal check.

Can a home Doppler tell me whether my baby has turned?

No. Sound location is unreliable, and hearing a heartbeat does not prove wellbeing. Any change in your baby’s usual movements needs prompt maternity advice.

My baby is breech at 30 weeks. Is a caesarean inevitable?

No. Many babies turn later. Your team will reassess and discuss a birth plan if breech presentation persists toward the end of pregnancy.

Is a posterior baby the same as a breech baby?

No. A posterior baby may still be head down but facing a different direction. Breech means the bottom or feet are nearest the birth canal.

Does engagement mean labour will start today?

No. Engagement describes the head moving into the pelvis, not a timetable for birth. Follow your maternity team’s advice about labour symptoms.

Can I turn the baby by pressing on my abdomen?

Do not attempt this yourself or with an untrained person. ECV needs assessment, monitoring and access to emergency care.

What if ECV does not work?

The team may discuss another attempt or plan birth with the baby still breech. Your preferences, pregnancy findings and the experience available locally all matter.

Can I still have a vaginal birth with a breech baby?

Sometimes, after specialist assessment and with an experienced hospital team. It is not suitable for every pregnancy, and the plan must include access to emergency caesarean delivery.

What should I do if my waters break while the baby is breech or transverse?

Call your maternity unit urgently and follow your agreed plan. Do not wait for strong contractions. If you see or feel the umbilical cord, call emergency services immediately.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
